newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage talks continue, four more freed.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage talks continue, four more freed.

text.p: Armed Peruvian rebels occupying the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima released four more captives on Thursday as negotiations continued over the fate of some 400 hostages still inside.

Witnesses at the scene reported earlier that two shots were heard at about 4:30 p.m. EST (2130 GMT) from inside the compound, which was seized on Tuesday by guerrillas representing the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
No information was available about the shots, which were followed by silence. There were no immediate reports of injuries.

The four male captives, all dressed in suits, were escorted from the residence at about 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) by Red Cross officials. One was later given a wheelchair, and they were driven away in a black car through a waiting crowd of journalists and onlookers.

A Red Cross official named the four men as Fidel Arraya, Carlos Chiapori, Juan Shimamabukuro and Setoti Kueochi. Chiapori was identified as an official with Japan's Nissan company. The nationalities of the four were not immediately known.

The guerrillas have threatened to kill their captives, which include many high-ranking diplomats, businessmen and government officials, if the Peruvian government does not release up to 500 of their jailed comrades.
Negotiations, headed by the Red Cross, which had two officials in the compound when the shots were heard, brought no early breakthrough in the crisis.
Michel Minning, a Swiss national of the Red Cross leading the talks, was also conducting a logistics operation to provide the hostages with basic supplies.

Four ambassadors, released on Wednesday as "hostages on parole", were also "acting as a link for commmunications between the Japanese residence and authorities outside," Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent told a news conference.
The other "hostages on parole" were the ambassadors of Germany, Heribert Woeckel, and Greece, Alcibiadis Karokis as well as a Peruvian ambassador, Armando Lecaros, Vincent said.

Minning, who has been in contact with the rebels since the assault, said the first priority was to continue providing those inside with food and other basic supplies. "We will address the question of the negotiations later," he said."
Vincent, who spent about 30 minutes in the compound early on Thursday, said: "Discussions were cordial, the hostages were in good condition.
"People are behaving magnificently ... Both the hostages and the members of the MRTA have behaved with restraint."
The hostages, all men since the release late on Tuesday of women captives, were sleeping on the floor in cramped conditions and living off a sparse diet of bread and water.
Vincent, who with the other released diplomats is channelling information to Peru's mediator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo Cabrejos, estimated there were about 400 hostages.
A letter faxed early on Wednesday from the residence to family members of hostages and signed by captives said there were 490 hostages. Six have been released since then.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said Washington was "very concerned" about the captives.
But in the morning, Minning said all inside were "fine, all calm."

Governments worldwide have urged Peru not to use force and to do everything in its power to protect the hostages. The embassy residence is legally Japanese territory, meaning in theory Fujimori would need Tokyo's approval for an assault.
Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda was reported to be flying from Tokyo to help in the negotiations, but it was not clear when he would arrive in Peru.
The German government, whose ambassador was released on Wednesday, urged Fujimori not to reject any chance to speak to the guerrillas.

The United States on Thursday sent a team of security advisers to Lima to assist the U.S. ambassador to Peru in the crisis, the State Department said. The ambassador and his deputy were at the reception, but left before the guerrillas struck. The State Department refused to comment on reports that six U.S. officials were among the hostages.
Fujimori, who ignored an ultimatum by the rebels for his presence on Wednesday, held his third emergency cabinet meeting since the crisis began.

The rebels, who included three non-Peruvians, assaulted the fortified compound from outside on Tuesday, linking up with comrades disguised as waiters inside a cocktail reception to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday, anti-terrorist police sources said. Cartridges were smuggled into the residence beforehand among flowers and inside Christmas cake.

The rebels released Fujimori's mother and sister, but were still believed to be holding one of his brothers. The president, the son of Japanese immigrants, may himself have narrowly escaped. He apparently was to attend the party, but was delayed on a trip to the provinces.
The captives also include Peru's foreign minister, agriculture minister, supreme court president and the current and past chiefs of the anti-terrorism police.
Attempts by the MRTA and the better-known Shining Path to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
